method: Inspected all 113 bracket-containing English quotation fields. Supplied short subjects, units, verse clauses and verbal complements are integrated into ordinary English. Referential appositives and all full authorial asides are retained as ordinary parentheses. Specific pronoun/apposition syntax is rewritten as documented. No Hebrew, anchor, source reference, connection decision or source fingerprint changes.

changes.before: The meaning of lighting the menorah is the statement, ‘Come and illuminate for Me as I illuminated for you,’ as written in Midrash Rabbah, Beha’alotcha and the beginning of Tetzaveh. This is the light of Oral Torah entrusted to Israel: ‘It is not in heaven.’ The same expression is found concerning Abraham our father: ‘Instead of illuminating for Me from Mesopotamia and its surroundings, come and illuminate before Me in the Land of Israel’; see there. This too is the light of Torah. The two thousand years of Torah began with Abraham, and he fulfilled and learned the entire Torah from what he understood in his heart. Bereshit Rabbah says that the Holy One appointed his two kidneys as two teachers, which flowed forth and taught him Torah. This means that he made God’s divinity known among created beings, as it says there: ‘Once I made Him known to His creatures, [He was called] God of the earth.’ This is the essence of words of Torah, for the root of all Torah is the utterance, ‘I am the Lord your God.’

changes.before: The essential achievement in the lighting of the lamps was that he was given the power to illuminate the light of Oral Torah, the meaning of ‘Come and illuminate before Me.’ Aaron received this power: through lighting the Temple lamps, he would cause the light of Oral Torah to appear and shine in the heart of all Israel. This is ‘Aaron did so: toward the front [of the menorah …].’ Rashi explains from Sifrei: ‘To tell Aaron’s praise, that he did not change.’ We do not find Scripture writing this about any other offering or commandment. Rather, it concerns the depth of the lamps’ intention: to illuminate the light of Oral Torah in Israel’s hearts. This was not stated explicitly in the command, but only alluded to.

changes.before: The Hasmoneans were then the root of Oral Torah, ‘a lawgiver from between his feet.’ The Gemara therefore says, ‘When the royal house of the Hasmoneans grew strong and defeated them,’ for victory came from the attribute of kingship, as the holy Zohar says that every weapon of war is entrusted into its hand. Their victory came through the aspect of kingship within them: they were the root of kingship, ‘the mouth—we call it Oral Torah.’ But when [the heretical idea] entered Yannai and he abolished all Oral Torah, as stated in Kiddushin, he took kingship only as a scepter of dominion. Therefore he was punished, and Yannai’s offspring came to an end when Herod’s rule began.

changes.before: They thought that selling Joseph would raise Judah’s strength to the height of tranquility and complete perfection. But when they saw Jacob’s mourning, and that this act had instead prevented tranquility—as explained above, through it they caused still greater damage—they brought Judah down from his greatness. They saw that he had not yet reached the perfection of greatness, and therefore had a deficiency. The sale itself also caused a greater deficiency and brought about his descent from greatness. Then Judah too began to return and regret what he had done, as our Sages said. Then began the light of the true Messiah, whose purpose is to make peace in the world; strife and division cannot come from him. [The first division within Israel, from Joseph, arose through an evil cause because of his level; likewise, as is known, division in the world comes from the division of David’s kingdom, through Jeroboam.] Judah recognized his deficiency in the fact that Joseph’s sale could come from him through hatred. [As with David’s sin concerning Uriah the Hittite, Judah’s true sin and deficiency lay only in this: that he too hated Joseph.] God forbid that the killing of Messiah son of Joseph should come through Israel; it comes only through Gog and Magog, who are the complete opposite of Messiah son of David, as is known. Therefore, when Judah returned from his hatred, this was the creation of the Messiah’s light. This is not the place to expand further; understand well.

changes.before: Their souls were therefore repaired through the subsequent birth of Peretz and Zerah. Peretz was Er’s soul, for peretz signifies forcefulness: ‘glory to him from the human [form],’ meaning that even if it is the opposite of glory in the eyes of other people, he does not heed that. Zerah was Onan’s soul, for his name indicates glory in the eyes of other people. Concerning these two, God said, ‘She is righteous; from Me’—‘From Me came the matters held concealed.’ Although Er and Onan were not fitting in His eyes, these two, who were their souls, were upright before Him. Although Peretz appears to act against the halakhah, as we find in David’s kingship, God testifies that this is because ‘It is a time to act for the Lord.’ Although in the deed Er’s sin appeared greater than Onan’s, his soul was greater in its depth than Onan’s, for David’s kingship was born from him. The Holy One conducts all the structures of David’s kingship through such structures, although at the time of the deed it appeared to him that he had sinned. Judah thought her a prostitute because she covered her face: the matter was a secret from God. As explained in the Midrash, ‘From Me came the matters held concealed’ means that the building of David’s kingship is a hidden secret, concealed even from prophets.

changes.before: The Talmud speaks of the ten utterances through which the world was created. It asks: there are only nine, and answers that ‘In the beginning’ is also an utterance. The whole creation is included in that utterance, but in the first utterance the creation does not yet have any apprehension. The first [explicitly spoken] utterance, ‘Let there be light,’ indicates that a person begins to recognize the difference between darkness and light. Afterward it says, ‘There was light’: the creation already recognizes the light, until the completion of the ten utterances, when the creation’s apprehension of God’s light has come into actuality. The person then sees that, from God’s side, everything was included before as well. The difference is only on his side: previously he was cut off from it, and now through his prayer he has attained deliverance. When a person attains deliverance through prayer, it is openly manifest. This is ‘The Lord attended to Sarah as He had said’: saying is in a whisper, as stated in the Zohar. ‘The Lord did for Sarah as He had spoken’: speech indicates that she has already attained deliverance through prayer, recognizing that God’s answer came through her prayer. It is then openly manifest, and is called speech.

changes.before: All the nations heard, ‘Peoples tremble’: after seeing open, explicit miracles they could not deny them. But [Amalek], through mockery, dismissed everything and denied it. This comes from pride: in his eyes it is impossible that anything should be hidden from his intellect and above his apprehension. Through this he becomes a scoffer and denies everything by mockery. This is ‘Amalek is the first of the nations,’ the beginning of the husk, for the root of the serpent’s enticement was ‘You will be like God.’ This is the utmost pride, as said concerning Nebuchadnezzar and Hiram, and it is the root of the evil inclination.

changes.before: Just as the root of every good thing is faith, with which the Torah opens, ‘I am …,’ not in the form of a command—and as explained in the Zohar on ‘This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous enter through it,’ the gate is the attribute of faith—so the root of every evil thing is scoffing. It is the opposite of faith, for it mocks everything. This is the meaning of ‘Amalek is the first of the nations,’ as the Midrash says: ‘Strike the scoffer’—this is Amalek; ‘and the simple person will become discerning’—this is Jethro. I heard that the simple person is one who believes everything, as it says, ‘The simple person believes every word.’ Jethro had left no form of idolatry [untried], as stated in the Mekhilta, for he believed everything. He can be repaired: through the striking of the scoffer, who believes nothing, he becomes discerning and believes in the true God. This is the beginning of all the evil groups among the nations, like ‘Laughter and lightheadedness accustom a person to sexual immorality.’

changes.before: Yet [Abraham] paid no attention to all this [the loss of reward and any enduring continuation], and cast his life aside for the love of God. He gave himself up in both worlds, agreeing that no continuation of him would remain. This was solely for his love of God; therefore his reward was doubled and redoubled. This awakened the holy Atika. The Holy One swore to him from the highest place, above all creatures, a place not joined to created beings. This is called the holy Atika, above human service, which is called Ze’ir Anpin. In truth, no human service reaches there, for His glory existed even before service existed: You are He before the world was created, and You are He after the world was created. From this place God shone upon Abraham, measure for measure, for his service too was above human power.

This is the essence of strength: ‘One who conquers his inclination.’ Through this he merits the joy of heart of those who seek God, for it says, ‘Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord.’ This is the joy that God desires in His world: ‘Let Israel rejoice in its Maker.’ It is possible only when the separating screen is removed. Thus it says both, ‘Serve the Lord with fear,’ and, ‘Serve the Lord with joy’: the two must be present together.

changes.before: When a person thinks that he has accomplished much in the service of God, he should know that he has not touched it at all. Thus the Gemara says, ‘A sign of arrogance is poverty in Torah,’ for ‘a coin in a jar rings noisily,’ unlike a full purse. Likewise the Zohar says, ‘The sign that one knows nothing is self-praise.’ This is not only boasting and arrogance before other people, but even privately, within one’s heart. The essence of pride is in the heart, as in ‘a lofty heart,’ when he thinks this way. Cain offered an inferior thing and thought he had performed a great service; therefore he was angry when it was not accepted. This error comes from forgetting the inclination and its power, and thinking that all the heart’s thoughts are only good, with no tendency to evil. God therefore informed him of the evil inclination: ‘Sin crouches at the door ….’ When he knows this and looks into the chambers of his heart, he will know that he has not acted in complete truth without any ulterior motive or self-interest. [God’s statement] ‘You can rule over it’ teaches that this too comes from God; understand.

changes.before: Therefore, although Moses did not understand Rabbi Akiva’s words, as stated in Menachot, his mind was settled when [the students] asked, ‘From where do you know this?’—perhaps you erred? [Rabbi Akiva] had to answer, ‘A halakhah to Moses from Sinai,’ for with Moses there is no error. In Rabbi Akiva’s wisdom, however, the wisdom of Oral Torah, clarification comes only when God illuminates his eyes that this ruling is a halakhah to Moses from Sinai. As the Sages say, everything that an accomplished student will eventually innovate was said to Moses at Sinai. This means that it is true wisdom [he finds where it is alluded to in Written Torah, for nothing is absent from its allusions; Written Torah is Moses’ wisdom, and there the matter is present at least by allusion]. That is, he recognizes and knows that it is certainly a halakhah to Moses from Sinai, and that his innovation is the innovation of an accomplished student.

changes.before: ‘These lamps we kindle for the deliverances, the miracles, and the wonders.’ ‘Miracles’ and ‘wonders’ apply to the miracle of the lamps that occurred then. But ‘deliverances’ belongs to the wars and does not concern the reason for the miracle of the lamps, which followed victory in battle. The double expression ‘miracles and wonders’ also needs explanation. A wonder, however, is something extraordinary and concealed from human reason. At the splitting of the sea it is written, ‘Working wonder’: human reason could not comprehend why Israel should cross the sea on dry land while the Egyptians drowned, for the accusation was, ‘How do these differ from those?’ The holy Zohar therefore says that the splitting of the sea depends upon Atika [the supernal, ancient source]. Hence the sayings, ‘A person’s sustenance is as difficult as the splitting of the sea,’ and ‘Matching them in marriage is as difficult as the splitting of the sea.’ For life, children, and sustenance depend not on merit but on mazal [here, the supernal source of their flow]—the attribute of ‘Nothingness,’ which is Israel’s mazal. We are attached to the root, high above the heights, where accusation has no power. This is ‘working wonder,’ beyond the grasp of human reason.

changes.before: From the side of faith, Israel believes in a general way without clear recognition: one believes even in what one does not comprehend at all. This is the definition of faith, as in ‘Your faithfulness in the nights’—in darkness and the concealment of the clear light, when faith is employed. In the morning, by contrast, [the blessing says] ‘True and firm’: truth is something completely clear to a person, against which no claim can be made, since it is visible to the eye. It comes from the apprehension of wisdom, as the Sages said, ‘There is no truth but Torah.’ Here distinctions exist: each is scorched by the apprehension of his fellow, and, as the Sages said, human minds are not alike. But faith amid concealment has no distinctions of level: all Israel believes, as the Sages said. This is the root of the congregation of Israel.

In the morning, by contrast, the blessing says ‘True and firm’: truth is something completely clear to a person, against which no claim can be made, since it is visible to the eye. It comes from the apprehension of wisdom, as the Sages said, ‘There is no truth but Torah.’ Here distinctions exist: each is scorched by the apprehension of his fellow, and, as the Sages said, human minds are not alike. But faith amid concealment has no distinctions of level: all Israel believes, as the Sages said. This is the root of the congregation of Israel.

changes.before: Moses therefore rejoiced when he heard them ask Rabbi Akiva, ‘Where do you have this from?’ and he answered, ‘It is a law given to Moses at Sinai.’ All the precious things Rabbi Akiva’s eye saw that Moses did not see belong to the wisdom of Oral Torah, of which Rabbi Akiva was the root, as Moses was of Written Torah. ‘A sage is superior to a prophet’: through the wisdom of Oral Torah one can attain every precious thing. Yet all of it is through an unilluminated speculum, being only the apprehension of one’s heart; a questioner can ask, ‘Where do you have this from? Perhaps you are mistaken.’ [Likewise, the Sages said concerning Ezekiel’s prophetic apprehension that the prophets too stand in this relation to Moses. The difference between prophetic apprehension—even that of the least prophet—and the wise apprehension of Oral Torah is like the difference between Moses’ prophecy and that of the other prophets: the latter, relative to his, is considered a seeing through the separation of several mirrors.] There is therefore disagreement in Oral Torah: through his wisdom one apprehends the matter differently, and all are the words of the living God. Human minds are not alike; God created differences in the lower beings’ apprehension of wisdom. But when he answers, ‘It is a law given to Moses at Sinai,’ [he refers to Moses,] who gazed through the illuminated speculum into supernal wisdom, in which there is no error, change, variation, or disagreement.

changes.before: Moses corresponded to ‘I am [the Lord your God],’ and Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef corresponded to ‘You shall have no [other gods].’ As is known, all the souls of Israel are attached at their root, each to the letters of Torah. Moses’ soul corresponded to ‘I am,’ and his work in this world was to clarify His blessed unity in the world. Rabbi Akiva’s soul corresponded to ‘You shall have no’: to clarify and cleanse every evil, dross, and waste in Israel’s heart, distancing them from evil, which is included in ‘You shall have no.’ His continual innovations of safeguards and fences added that this too is included in ‘You shall have no’ and must also be cleansed. All the laws of prohibited and permitted, invalid and valid, impure and pure, separate evil from good. This explains the Talmud’s account: when Moses ascended on high he found the Holy One tying crowns to the letters. He asked, ‘Master of the universe, who is delaying You?’ He answered, ‘After several generations there will be a man called Akiva ben Yosef, who will expound heaps of laws from every stroke.’ Moses became distressed, until they reached one law. Asked where it came from, [Rabbi Akiva] answered, ‘It is a law given to Moses at Sinai.’ Moses had seen Rabbi Akiva expand ‘You shall have no,’ adding many safeguards, and became distressed. Yet it is known that the root of everything is ‘I am the Lord your God’; ‘You shall have no’ is only a protection against a person distancing himself from the Lord his God. This is why he became distressed. When he reached one law—that is, when Moses saw why so many safeguards were necessary—he was told, ‘A law given to Moses at Sinai.’ ‘One law’ means ‘I am,’ for this is Torah’s essence, as the Zohar says: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one’ is a great essential principle of Torah. ‘You shall have no’ serves only to guard Israel from departing from ‘I am the Lord your God.’ His mind was then settled, for he understood that the essential principle had been given to him.

He too was the head of his generation, encompassing all its souls, and completed himself to the utmost in all the levels of his stature. changes.before: We have already said that at the departure of the holy Shabbat, before Havdalah, six expressions of deliverance are recited. On Shabbat, ‘I am the Lord who sanctifies you’: God Himself bestows holiness. When Shabbat departs, the holiness recedes. We therefore ask through six verses of deliverance, corresponding to the six working days, that this become fixed in the heart, as explained concerning Havdalah in Bereshit. So too at Chanukah: the light comes from God, and deliverance is needed for it to remain fixed in the heart afterwards. These are ‘the deliverances’ that occurred then. Through the miracle’s illumination, which came from God, He established permanence in the heart, a deliverance for afterwards as well. At the beginning of ‘These lamps,’ the order is ‘deliverances, miracles, and wonders’; at the end it is ‘for Your miracles, Your wonders, and Your deliverances,’ with deliverance last. Everything begins through God’s help and deliverance, so ‘deliverances’ comes first. For the deliverance to be established for all time, even after the season passes, it is mentioned last, so that His deliverance never leaves us. At the beginning, God’s illumination becomes fixed in the heart through the person’s beginning to light: through human action it is immediately fixed in the heart, in all one’s powers. Thus in the initial act, deliverance came first, followed by the miracles and wonders, which occurred after the act of lighting through human action. On leaving [the festival], deliverance is said last, for its disclosure comes after the days of Chanukah have passed.

changes.before: Damage above through sins is like what we call an eclipse of the sun. In truth the sun, in itself and from its own side, suffers no eclipse at all; the absence of its light upon the earth is called an eclipse of the sun. Since its purpose is to illuminate the earth, this counts as an impairment on its side. Every night is likewise an eclipse of the sun, for this too comes through an intervening screen, like its eclipse by day. Nevertheless, when the moon shines, the sun’s eclipse is not complete: as is known, the moon’s light comes from the sun and the radiance of its light. Although we call it moonlight, those who understand know that it is really sunlight and has not been completely eclipsed. At the end of the month, or when the moon too is eclipsed and does not shine, the sun’s eclipse is complete. This is precisely an analogy for above: ‘More than the calf [wants to suckle, the cow wants to nurse].’ The purpose of the unfolding of Atzilut is to bestow upon Israel. When Israel sins and does not receive the light of knowing God fully, this is counted, as it were, as weakness in the heavenly retinue. This is the meaning of destruction above, exile compared to night, and the levels within exile itself. Understand all this.

changes.before: He [Abraham] therefore asked God to help him through the holiness present in his inborn nature, called ‘his sister,’ so that it would guard him from faltering, Heaven forbid. Here, after he had accomplished much in holiness through his trials and good deeds, reaching completion in circumcision, he prayed that all the holiness he had acquired until then should become fixed within him as ‘my sister’: that Israel should possess holiness even without conscious awareness, which could never be lost in any way. Even if he enters doubts and concealments, that holiness will not enter doubt, and he will begin anew to serve God and acquire more holiness through his own toil. As the Sages said, Israel is recognizable through these three signs—compassion, bashfulness, and kindness—which were fixed in Israel’s heart by birth as an inheritance from the holy patriarchs.

changes.before: This is also the Sages’ statement: it is received as tradition that Amalek falls only through Rachel’s descendants. Rachel’s descendants indicate intensified service through great self-restraint. Thus, before the completeness of David’s kingship had been achieved, when Amalek stood against them, they needed a king from Rachel’s descendants. So too, ‘Moses took Joseph’s bones with him’: Joseph’s bones indicate great self-restraint. Israel had not yet attained completeness, and the accusation remained at their departure from Egypt, ‘These [served idols], and those [served idols].’ God nevertheless testified for them: ‘When you bring the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God.’ As long as Israel travels the road toward acquiring completeness, before reaching it, Amalek stands along that road in accusation—‘who encountered you on the road.’ The only counsel against him then is Joseph’s bones, intensified service. If they rest even a little, he immediately misleads through his accusation.

changes.before: The Talmud mentions ‘that he should not kick against [those greater than him]’ because this is Torah’s intended purpose: that through Torah his spirit should become lowly, and he should not kick against someone greater. Thus the holy Torah’s utmost humility appears in those souls who were the roots of Torah wisdom. Abraham said, ‘I am dust and ashes,’ and the Sages said that God supplied him with his two kidneys as two teachers, which flowed and taught him Torah. Moses and Aaron said, ‘What are we?’ and they were the roots of Written and Oral Torah. King David said, ‘I am a worm’; he too is a root of Oral Torah, being a vehicle for kingship—‘the mouth, Oral Torah.’ Precisely because words of Torah became fixed in their hearts, they reached the utmost lowliness within their souls.

changes.before: Thus concerning Moses it says, ‘The man Moses was exceedingly humble.’ Surely Moses knew that he was the greatest of all Israel: he himself wrote the Torah from the Holy One’s mouth, including ‘No prophet arose [again like Moses].’ He therefore knew very well that he was the greatest. Rather, he clearly recognized that no power of existence is present in the world apart from God, for there is nothing besides Him. Because he recognized this so clearly, he was the receptive vessel for every kind of divine light. He knew that all the greatness within him was not from himself at all, but from God, who chose him. Had God chosen another soul of Israel, that other soul could have been the greatest and most distinguished of all Israel. Of this recognition it says, ‘The man Moses was exceedingly humble.’ This is why he was the vessel to receive every kind of light.

changes.before: This is the saying, ‘A cluster—the One to whom everything belongs’: the Creator of everything, including the aspect called evil just explained. ‘He atones for the sin of the kid’—the aspect of darkness in creation—so that it becomes ‘very good.’ This is what the Sages indicated when they said that the eshkolot ceased. All the eshkolot from Moses’ time until Yose ben Yoezer’s death learned Torah like Moses: through Torah they had the power to turn creation’s evil into ‘very good,’ like Moses, to whom God said at that event [the calf], ‘Now leave Me alone,’ making it depend upon him. They too were therefore called eshkolot, ‘those containing everything’: through their Torah they could make the aspect of ‘everything’ become very good.

changes.before: When it becomes clear that even at the time of imagination he is truly attached to God, and he takes this to heart—knowing that he has no power to think or contemplate anything except from God—the imagination is consequently repaired. As the Sages said, ‘The One to whom everything belongs atones for the sin of the kid’: everything belongs to Him, all deeds, actions, thoughts, and desires; therefore the sin too belongs to Him, and He consequently atones. With the very faculty of imagination in which fantasy grows strong, one prevails against it, to consume and annul it. Thus the root of Amalek, the pursuer, becomes pursued through itself. The document he wrote, ‘That the Jews should …,’ had its interpretation reversed in the second documents, revealing the intention that they should rule over their enemies; and the gallows prepared for Mordecai were turned against him. The apparent victory of imagination was afterwards reversed: it became clear that false imagination had not prevailed, but actual truth. Joseph’s dreams are an example: at the time they appeared imaginary; afterwards, when events occurred accordingly, it became clear that they had not been fantasy at all. This is the visible analogy. There are many levels, higher than one another, in elevating and repairing thoughts and imaginings so that imagination becomes truth. The essential thing is clear recognition that ‘there is nothing besides Him,’ that everything is His, and that human wisdom and schemes are nothing. So too in drunkenness, when one lacks the understanding and wisdom of sobriety: since it is God alone who brings forth counsel, thought, and desire within him, everything is thereby repaired. Concerning this it says, ‘When [the Lord] gives rest.’ First a person must labor to remove the seven evil qualities revealed in his heart, so that he should not come to an actual transgression, Heaven forbid, or to thoughts of transgression revealed in his heart. Once he is clean of this, he should then labor to erase vain imaginings from within his heart.

The document he wrote, ‘That the Jews should …,’ had its interpretation reversed in the second documents, revealing the intention that they should rule over their enemies; and the gallows prepared for Mordecai were turned against him. The apparent victory of imagination was afterwards reversed: it became clear that false imagination had not prevailed, but actual truth. Joseph’s dreams are an example: at the time they appeared imaginary; afterwards, when events occurred accordingly, it became clear that they had not been fantasy at all. This is the visible analogy. There are many levels, higher than one another, in elevating and repairing thoughts and imaginings so that imagination becomes truth. The essential thing is clear recognition that ‘there is nothing besides Him,’ that everything is His, and that human wisdom and schemes are nothing. So too in drunkenness, when one lacks the understanding and wisdom of sobriety: since it is God alone who brings forth counsel, thought, and desire within him, everything is thereby repaired. changes.before: The intention is as stated: Torah’s purpose is that everything be in Israel’s hands. This apparently resembles the way of the nations, who say, ‘My strength and the power of my hand [made this wealth for me],’ while Israel takes the opposite position, recognizing that everything comes from God. Yet because the nations, thinking that effort was in their hands, did not wish to accept the effort of Torah, their very notion of effort instead brought an absence of effort. Israel, possessing the recognition of an absence of [independent] effort, accepted effort. From this it follows that their claim is justified: it should be considered theirs and their effort. This is like the Sages’ statement, ‘Eventually it is called his Torah.’

Yet the Sages also praise aged Torah scholars, and elders are praised elsewhere. In truth they said, ‘I learned much from my teachers … and from my students more …’. ‘From my teachers’ refers to the beginning and desire. Attainment, however, comes from God, for ‘the Lord gives wisdom,’ and everything is in Heaven’s hands except fear of Heaven. The latter is the receptive, feminine attribute and the awakening from below through desire and will; it is in the person’s hands, and therefore is good and great.

changes.before: He [Isaac] is the beginning of Torah’s disclosure, for Torah comes forth from the side of might. Although Abraham himself fulfilled the whole Torah and his two kidneys flowed with Torah, the principal meaning of the name Torah is instruction, directing a way for others. This was not yet clarified in Abraham, for nothing remained among all those he taught. Only what he later taught his son Isaac endured forever. In Isaac we find no further ‘souls that he made’ and taught to others, because the power of restraint was already within him: to limit the outflow, so as not to teach and bestow a Torah of kindness upon those outside or unworthy of it. He taught only his children. Yet even among them was one unworthy, although he is called an apostate Israelite in Kiddushin 18a: he possessed a Jewish root from birth. Thus his head is buried in the Cave of Machpelah in Isaac’s bosom, on account of ‘the game in his mouth’: the souls of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Meir, roots of Oral Torah. The Mishnah is the foundation of Oral Torah; an anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, and all follow Rabbi Akiva’s approach. Thus even within him there was some attachment to Torah, but ultimately there was refuse as well. Torah’s completeness was in Jacob, whose offspring were whole: completeness in truth, which is Torah. Nevertheless, it comes forth from the side of might; the root of that emergence had already begun in Isaac.

Therefore the totality of Oral Torah was then revealed in the composition of the Mishnah, which potentially includes everything that later generations’ sages will innovate.

He thought that he had already completed the repair, and sought to dwell in tranquility, seeing his world during his lifetime, something like the World to Come. changes.before: The meaning is that when [Abraham] saw them give way before one another [the opposing powers described above], he understood that the blessed God had not concealed Himself completely. God therefore established two opposites, so that through both people would recognize that there is One higher than them who rules them, and would look only toward Him. For this reason God also established male and female in every matter in the world. Likewise it is written, ‘Lift your eyes on high and see: Who created these?’ ‘These’ means all the particulars that God established in the world. ‘Who’ is the place open to questioning: a person should seek to know Who created these. For this purpose God created all the particulars called ‘these,’ as stated in the introduction to the holy Zohar, 1b, and as explained in the portion of Bereshit. God desires that created beings ask Who the Creator is; He therefore created opposing things in the world.

changes.before: To the extent that a person distances himself from evil—that is, from all the attractions of this world and desires directed toward himself—he draws close to God and attains His light, as it says, ‘Bring us back, and cause Your face to shine.’ Conversely, to the extent that he attains awareness of God, he distances himself from worldly matters, as expressed by ‘I am’ and ‘You shall have no other.’ Of this they said, ‘If there is no awe, there is no wisdom; if there is no wisdom, there is no awe.’ Wisdom is apprehension of God, and awe is fear of sin; neither suffices without the other. Awe is called a storehouse and a vessel of reception: the heart empties itself of all kinds of desires and attractions and thereby becomes an empty vessel to receive words of Torah. As our Sages say: when a word of mockery leaves, a word of Torah enters; when a word of Torah leaves, a word of mockery enters. When the heart is empty of Torah, it is ready to receive every kind of desire, for it cannot remain wholly empty. Therefore the two go together. Neither precedes the other beyond an instant; the other level follows immediately. When a person turns his heart toward God, God immediately causes His light to rest there. Awe is what God asks of people, as it says, ‘What does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear’; wisdom is what God bestows, as it says, ‘He gives wisdom to the wise,’ and, ‘For the Lord gives wisdom.’ The awakening from below must come first. Of this they said, ‘Open for Me like the point of a needle’: even the smallest awe suffices, and a corresponding measure of wisdom will then flow into the heart. Through the wisdom more awe comes, then more wisdom, and so on, until there are openings [large enough for wagons and carriages to enter, as the cited Midrash continues]. The early teachers said: provided that the opening passes through from side to side. This means a complete awakening from the depths of the heart to abandon sin and relinquish all worldly concerns; even a single moment is enough.

changes.before: This was the matter with Jacob our father when he heard the news that Joseph was still alive, as it says, “The spirit of Jacob revived.” He feared for himself lest this joy be merely a joy of this world, and therefore tested and refined himself through these clarifications. The first clarification was his saying, “I will go and see him before I die,” corresponding to “A person should always stir [the good inclination against the evil inclination],” as explained. The second was “He offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac,” corresponding to “He should occupy himself with Torah,” like the blessing we recite each day, “Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to occupy ourselves with words of Torah.” For in giving the Torah, the Holy One is called Gevurah: “Thus Moses heard from the mouth of the Gevurah,” as is known to the discerning. There Jacob was told, “I will surely bring you up as well,” corresponding to “I am the Lord your God who brought you out”: the latter concerns the past, while the former concerns the future. His sending Judah ahead, which our Sages interpreted as establishing a house of study, also belonged to this matter. He then underwent the third clarification: “He wept upon his neck further,” which our Sages expounded as teaching that he recited the Shema. Afterwards he said to Joseph, “Now I may die,” corresponding to the fourth counsel, to remind himself of the day of death. When Jacob saw that after all these the joy remained, he understood that it came from God and was true joy, enduring forever.

changes.before: The Talmud relates that he saw [his colleague] being especially cheerful and said, “It is written, ‘Rejoice with trembling.’” He replied, “I am wearing tefillin.” What did this answer? One may not fill one’s mouth with laughter in this world, and it is written, “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter”—specifically then! Tefillin indicate attachment to the root of thought: “In the beginning”—for the sake of Israel. Israel crown the Holy One with the splendor of tefillin, proclaiming “The Lord is one,” and the Holy One praises Israel’s excellence. Thus “all the peoples of the earth will see that the Lord’s name is called upon you” refers to the tefillin of the head. “Upon you” is precise: the head tefillin are like a crown upon the head. The Zohar explains that the word az, “then,” indicates the illumination of Atika: the alef pierces the darkness and reaches the zayin—alef-zayin. This is “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter.” In the future the aspect signified by “He” will be disclosed and illuminate; hence “on that day,” when the aspect called “He,” indicating Atika, will shine like day. Specifically then our mouth will be filled with laughter. This is the answer, “I am wearing tefillin”: when a Jew puts on tefillin, a disclosure of Atika’s light shines within him through his attachment to the root. This too is “then.”

changes.before: Therefore they said that a good person is given a taste of the fruit of his deeds in this world: at intervals God illuminates for a person, his heart begins to burn with enthusiasm, and he actually feels life in his heart, while his soul rejoices in God. For the essence of life is joy, as explained in the Zohar at the end of Vayakhel concerning “in sorrow,” which signifies death. Of Shabbat, which is a taste of the World to Come, our Sages expounded in Bereshit Rabbah, “‘He adds no sorrow with it’—this is the mourner.” Therefore on Shabbat it says, “Delight in the Lord,” and the Zohar reads “in” as literally “above”: it is the meal of Atika Kadisha. The divine name indicates sensing God before one’s eyes, within the defined form of Torah. On Shabbat, however, a person can delight expansively, above that level of apprehension, with the expansiveness of joy that carries one beyond the usual boundaries through the heart’s widening. This is the meal of Atika Kadisha: the joy we experience through attachment to the hidden root, a taste of the World to Come in the expansion of delights. Even what appears directed toward oneself is all for the honor of Heaven, since one is attached to the hidden root. Thus at the beginning of the chapter Ein Omdin, when he saw [his colleague] being especially cheerful, the reply was, “I am wearing tefillin.” The head that bears tefillin signifies attachment to the hidden root, as explained above and in the Tikkunim’s Patach Eliyahu; from this comes the great joy. Therefore tefillin are called a sign, as is Shabbat: both signify the hidden root that distinguishes Israel from idolaters, like the sign of the covenant.

changes.before: “These lights … [we may do nothing with them] except look at them, in order to give thanks …”: this follows what is written, “Open for me the gates of righteousness; I shall enter them and thank Yah. This is the gate of the Lord ….” When a person merits having the gates of righteousness opened in the heart through the shining revelation of the glory of His kingship, this brings thanksgiving and praise to God. It is like “My Lord, open my lips”—these are the gates of righteousness—and thereby “my mouth will declare Your praise.” How does one merit this? The verse says, “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous enter it.” Through the repair of the holiness of the covenant, which is the quality of the righteous one, a person merits the illumination of the gates of righteousness within the heart, as it says, “Light is sown for the righteous.” Through this one comes to give thanks and praise.

changes.before: This is the illumination of the Chanukah lamp that was established for all generations: by this light, to eliminate every kind of mixture from Israel. Such mixture follows from the inward powers of Israel being mingled with mixed desires, whose being solely for the sake of Heaven—and not for some other thought or ulterior motive—has not been clarified, as befits the root of the Jewish people, the congregation of Israel, who are completely attached to the living God. In truth, all the power of Yesod comes from Netzach and Hod; if Yesod is clarified, Netzach and Hod are also clarified. But in Yesod this is actually manifest, whereas in Netzach and Hod it remains potential: its emergence into actuality is still concealed. Concealment leaves room for error, and a lamp is needed to illuminate. Therefore “above twenty [cubits] it is invalid, because the eye does not take it in”: it still remains concealed. The essential purpose of the Chanukah lamp is to bring what is concealed into revelation.

changes.before: When [Joseph] was thrown into the pit of snakes and scorpions and did not kill them, he knew that they had been sent to kill him and that a miracle had been performed for him. It was therefore punished with “dust is the serpent’s bread,” deprived of the taste of the desire for food. The scorpion certainly kills, as Berakhot 33a states, “For a scorpion, however, one interrupts [prayer].” It corresponds to the blemish of murder that extended through Cain, and to the blemish of a limb from a living animal. Even the nations take care about this because of its great cruelty, apart from the prohibition placed upon the descendants of Noah; this is why Nebuchadnezzar was ashamed when he ate a living hare, as stated in Nedarim 65a. When the snakes and scorpions appeared before Joseph, he sensed that he needed clarification concerning his slander, and he certainly repented for the two blemishes mentioned above.

changes.before: When God wishes to test a person, He causes the person to forget the full severity of the prohibition concerning the matter in which He wishes to test him. This was also the matter of the tribes [Joseph’s brothers]. When they wished to kill him, the whole prohibition was concealed from them. Only through counsel other than words of Torah was he saved from their hands, and they too were saved from sin. Judah was very wise in worldly matters; he therefore devised advice and said, “What profit?” Even though it appeared to him that killing him was legally permitted, as will be explained, what benefit would come to us from it? [Would my father give me the striped coat? The striped coat belongs specifically to Joseph. Supplement.] Would our father love us more because of this? As soon as they agreed not to kill him, they saw the gravity of the prohibition: killing him was also legally forbidden. A person may not use this advice based on worldly wisdom as his protection at all times, but only at the time of a test when no other counsel is available. When one remembers that something is prohibited, it is forbidden to withdraw from it on the basis of such advice; one must withdraw because of His command. This explains the Gemara: “Anyone who blesses Judah”—meaning that he approves of acting this way always—“is called one who compromises.” Judah, too, used this advice only at the time of the test.

changes.before: But [Joseph’s] words were “only a loss,” through his saying to the chief cupbearer, “Remember me” and “mention me.” He did not regard this as any sin, for he really did not put his trust in the chief cupbearer—as it says, “Who places his trust in the Lord”: this is Joseph. Rather, because he sensed that the cause of his deliverance would in fact be the chief cupbearer, he wanted the deliverance to come about through nature, since one does not rely on a miracle. Nevertheless, it was a loss to him: two years were added, to awaken him regarding the words with which he had slandered his brothers, which had likewise seemed a slight matter to him. In truth, the two blemishes mentioned above branched out from this, for malicious speech and slander come from jealousy and anger, and the covenant of the tongue corresponds to the covenant of the sexual organ, as is known. Such words are among the sins a person treads underfoot, and they bring only loss. Through this, two years were added to awaken him to the need to repair the blemish of the two days through [the correction of] his words. This is hinted at by “At the end of two years of days”: when the blemish of the two days was repaired, “Pharaoh dreamed,” as it says, “Until the time his word came; the word of the Lord refined him.”

This comes from Isaac’s power and quality. Generosity comes from the quality of love, “kindness to Abraham,” which is its very opposite. If so, on the contrary, their eyes [the brothers’] are more generous, and they possess a better eye than he does.

changes.before: In the havdalah within prayer the wording is, “You taught us to perform the statutes of Your will”; similarly, in Al HaNissim we say, “to make them forget Your Torah and turn them away from the statutes of Your will.” It seems that this hints at what the Ari’s writings suggest through the letters chet, shin, mem in Chashmonai: chodesh, Shabbat, milah—month, Sabbath, circumcision—which they wished to abolish from Israel. These three commandments are called “the statutes of Your will” because they are engraved specifically as a sign within the souls of Israel, through which they are distinguished from the nations. For this reason the Greeks arose to abolish specifically these three commandments from Israel, since Israel’s holiness is engraved precisely through them. Concerning the holiness of Shabbat it is written, “Between Me and the children of Israel it is a sign forever.” The holiness of circumcision likewise is a sign specifically for Israel, as is known; as Nedarim 31b states, “[One who vows] that I may not benefit from the circumcised is forbidden [to benefit] from uncircumcised Israelites ….” The holiness of the month also belongs specifically to Israel, as it says, “This month is for you.” Although the calculation of the new moon is known to everyone, this power was given specifically to Israel: they can sanctify the month even before the conjunction or after it. As Rosh Hashanah 25a says, “‘You’—even when mistaken; ‘you’—even when deliberate ….”

changes.before: This is why the Second Temple was built through the kings of Persia. As is written in Berakhot 8b [in praise of] the Persians, “They are modest …”: this was their holy spark, the quality of modesty. But the Gemara immediately brings the statement, “These are the Persians consecrated for Gehinnom,” for it is forbidden to recount the praise of idolaters, as stated in Avodah Zarah 20a. In truth, their own excellence is what brings them to Gehinnom, because their modesty is for the purpose of satisfying their desire all the more, and also because of the evil eye and begrudging disposition they possessed, as explained above. Similarly, concerning Ahasuerus—whose royal power is greater because it encompasses the entire nation—the Sages say, “From the disgrace of that wicked man you learn his praise …,” also concerning modesty. But this is truly his disgrace, as above, since his intention is wholly disgraceful. Nevertheless, for Israel it is good. Esther merited it, as the Sages said, “In reward for the modesty that she possessed ….” She absorbed the good quality of modesty, “Walk modestly with your God,” which likewise means remaining concealed rather than revealed.

As it says there, “He smelled the fragrance of his garments,” and the Sages said, “Do not read ‘his garments’ but ‘his traitors’”—that is, the bad odor of the goats’ strong scent. A good fragrance also benefits the neighbors, as illustrated by the comparison of naphtha and balsam. This is Israel’s excellence: “When Samaria was cursed, its neighbors were blessed; when Babylonia was cursed, its neighbors were cursed …,” as stated in the second chapter of Eruvin. This is like “Woe to the wicked [and woe to his neighbor]” at the end of Sukkah. Israel’s essential quality is a good fragrance. As the Sages say concerning “My nard gave its fragrance,” even with reference to the calf, this was not false. This is also why they expounded “the fragrance of his garments” as “his traitors”: even their wicked one has a good fragrance. For Israel and Torah are one; just as Torah has the excellence of fragrance, so does Israel.

changes.before: Why did the Sages say, “You might say their hope is lost …,” when nothing stands in the way of repentance? This initial possibility follows the holy Zohar’s statements that repentance for this blemish is difficult. It depends on the first blemish—the serpent’s instigation—being completely clarified, so that deliberate sins become merits. The death that the serpent brought into the world would then cease as a consequence. That clarification cannot occur in this world until the days of the Messiah, when we merit eternal life. This is the Messiah’s light: “He asked life of You; You gave him length of days forever and ever.” Then the Messiah will “smell and judge,” as Sanhedrin 93b says, because the quality of fragrance and purity will be completely perfected: “His sensing [by scent] is in the fear of the Lord.” Therefore they said, “Scripture says, ‘The mandrakes have given fragrance’: both these and those will in the future give fragrance.” Even one who has, Heaven forbid, blemished this always has hope and repair, by taking care to turn his heart and eyes away from evil thoughts and continually entering into the occupation of Torah. As Maimonides says at the end of the laws of forbidden intercourse, “Thoughts of forbidden relations grow strong only in a heart empty of wisdom.” Through occupation in Torah one merits holy sight, as it says, “Your eyes shall see your teachers.” The word Torah means that it instructs a person in the revelation of the glory of His blessed name. Through this one merits the fragrance of purity: “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.” Occupation in Torah is the consummation of repentance and the repair of the blemish mentioned above. The word yirah, fear, hints at repentance, as they expounded, “‘Happy is the man who fears the Lord’—happy is one who repents while still a man.” They likewise said, “The purpose of wisdom is repentance …,” for “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.” Through Torah study it is always possible for the blemish to be repaired even in this world, as it says, “Healing to all his flesh.” And “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever” refers to Torah, as the holy Zohar explains: it remains with a person forever, purifying him and refining his soul so that he merits a spirit of purity.

changes.before: We have said that the eight days of Chanukah also indicate completeness from Binah to Malkhut: from the will within the heart, for a person is responsible for having the heart’s desire, the quality of “Binah is the heart.” Afterward, the seven qualities—the instruments of action—are completed with God’s help, as it says, “The Lord will complete [the matter] for me … do not abandon the works of Your hands.” Thus the quality of Malkhut is completed on the eighth day of Chanukah. The name Zot Chanukah certainly fits the revelation of the kingship of Heaven. As is known, zeh and zot indicate the unification of the Holy One and His Divine Presence; as Ra’aya Meheimna says, “He is truth and she is faith.” Zeh indicates something standing clearly before one’s eyes. As the Mekhilta and the holy Zohar say, “A maidservant at the sea saw what Ezekiel did not see”: each person pointed with a finger and said, “This is my God ….” Likewise, in the future, when the apprehension of divinity is clear before every eye, all the screens pass away, and truth in its fullness is revealed, the Sages say: “The Holy One will make a circle for the righteous … and each will point with his finger,” as it says, “It will be said on that day: Behold, this is our God, for whom we hoped, and He saved us; this is the Lord ….” This is “on that day”: the quality of “He” will be revealed like daylight.

changes.before: An ordinary expression that a person habitually uses, a saying constantly on his lips, is actual words of Torah—even in the case of an ordinary person of Israel. Thus we often find the Talmud citing “as people say,” and this is words of Torah. In the first chapter of Sanhedrin there are many instances of “That person who used to go about saying …,” followed by Samuel saying, “It is written in Scripture.” For every soul of Israel has its own particular attachment to words of Torah, as is known, and the expression constantly on a person's lips is the root of his soul. [For speech is the foundation of the soul: “a living soul” is translated “a speaking spirit”; and, as stated in the Pesikta, the only difference between living and dead righteous people is speech—this is the foundation of vitality.] From this a person can discern the root of his soul and know what his task is in this world.

changes.before: The language of blessing was not used at the outset, because what [Jacob] would say to them was not yet clear to him. But our teacher Moses began immediately with “And this is the blessing,” because the word vezot indicates that everything was clear to him as soon as he began to speak. With Jacob, vezot appears only after all the blessings, because only then, after all his words, was it clear to him that all his blessings came from God; this was not clear beforehand. At first God placed words of reproach in his mouth, to reproach the first three tribes, for a Torah scholar must take vengeance and retain a grievance. When he reached the tribe of Judah, God showed him from Heaven that he should forgo the strict measure of his response. For the letters of Judah contain the Divine Name, and the dalet in his name alludes to the verse, “But to this one I will look: to one poor and broken in spirit, who trembles at My word.” This means one who understands that, of himself, he has nothing, as it is stated, “The dalet gathers [what it receives].” Therefore there was no place here for anger or wrath to take hold. When the quality of mercy opened in Judah, it prevailed over the other tribes as well, and they were all included in the blessing.

changes.before: My father of blessed memory explained that the contributions for the communal offerings allude to the first will by which God chose Israel, as in the statement that Israel arose first in thought. In that place no superiority of one person over another applies; therefore all Israel gave equally in this contribution. The contribution for the sockets indicates the completion of clarification, as in the Talmudic statement, “All Israel have a portion in the world to come.” Here too no superiority of one over another applies, which is why all Israel gave equally in this contribution as well. The contribution for the Tabernacle indicates the service God established in this world. Here it was “everyone whose heart moved him”: according to each person's work in his service, his exertion and hardship, his breaking through concealment and clarifying why God chose him, so he sees God dwelling with him. In this service they cannot be equal: one may, Heaven forbid, be distant and another near, according to his service. Therefore [Moses] made the hooks of the pillars from the surplus of the contribution for the sockets. As the Zohar states, they were made in the form of a vav; and the Zohar says that vav joins the upper world to the lower—that is, it joins God's will to a person's limited apprehension. These hooks were made from the surplus of the sockets' contribution, which alludes to the completed clarification, to show that in the depth every Israelite recognizes the connection of His light with his own apprehension, since in the depth each has “one point that always reaches.” In truth, all Israel have a portion in the world to come. What does this imply? Even in this world, where God established that a person sees the Holy One dwelling within him according to his service—as the Tabernacle contribution indicates—nevertheless, in the depth no soul of Israel will be rejected, and each recognizes the connection of God's light with his own apprehension.

changes.before: The matter is that God clothed His light in the garments and deeds of the commandments. A person who wishes to attain God's light attains it by fulfilling His will in the activity and deeds of the commandments. One must necessarily proceed through those acts and deeds; intention alone is insufficient. If intention alone were sufficient, why did God command the commandments at all? This shows that through intention alone a person cannot reach God's light, but only through practical commandments, through which he attains it. Then he sees clearly that even the power of this action is also God's. Holiness is then established within him permanently, so that he always sees clearly before his eyes that every power of action comes from God. This lasting holiness that a person establishes through fulfilling His will in the garments and deeds of the commandments is called Torah, as it is written, “For a commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light.” By fulfilling His will in the deeds of the commandments he attains God's light completely and sees that God acts in all things: even the power of his own service comes from God. This permanence is called Torah. When a person reaches this completeness, and this holiness has already been established within him, he truly needs no action [to attain this recognition]. At first he must proceed through the acts and deeds of the commandments; but when, through fulfilling His will, he has established such holiness within himself and recognizes that all the power of his actions comes from God—this is called Torah—he needs no action [to attain it]. Thus the Talmud says: “A commandment, at the time he is engaged in it, protects and saves …; Torah, both when he is engaged in it and when he is not, protects and saves.” For with a commandment, it is only while engaged in it that he sees God's light, whereas Torah means the holiness he has permanently established through the commandments, and this permanence is always with him. Although with words of Torah we also find, “Should you let your eyes flit from it, it is gone,” implying that even words of Torah sometimes cease from him, this is only when a person turns his attention away and proceeds with self-assurance: since he already possessed this recognition called Torah, [he thinks] he no longer needs any service. Then it is written, “Should you let your eyes flit from it, it is gone.” But when a person does not turn his attention away, he possesses it permanently, both when he is engaged in it and when he is not.

changes.before: Therefore, in the wording of “Al HaNissim,” the kindling of the lamps is singled out from all the services, because this is the principal completion of the quality of Hod that they repaired then. The miracle they experienced in this is not mentioned, because it is not the matter of Chanukah's miracle and deliverance, but what Heaven revealed to them: that they had been accepted before Him and had repaired completely, to the point that Heaven assisted them in giving light before Him. From this they understood to establish the days of Chanukah for all generations, kindling lamps also outside the Temple, throughout the country. After the destruction there is also a lamp for each person, or at least “a lamp for a person and his household,” with which to illuminate all who enter the world. Therefore its principal placement is outside, to illuminate the world. Only when [Israel] became intermingled among the nations was this light concealed; thus we light inside the house, as in a time of danger, which is likewise a time when the nations are aroused to decrees of forced apostasy arising from Israel's association with them. So too we are now continually, through our many sins, very closely associated with them—to the point that they said in Avodah Zarah that Israel outside the Land serve idolatry in purity, and even permitted the food and drink of their festivals and similar matters. The light is not openly manifest outside, yet it nevertheless illuminates within. For in truth, in the depths of the heart this light of Hod shines, and all their association is in purity. This has already been repaired through Mattathias, at the first decree of forced apostasy against Israel: it was clarified that the depths of Israel's hearts are forever attached to God, and that their association with the nations, in the deepest truth, is only to absorb holy sparks from them. As they said in Pesachim, Israel were exiled only so that converts might be added to them—not necessarily actual converts, but the added absorption of the nations' powers, returning them to holiness little by little, until the final time when everything returns to holiness. Although this is not yet outwardly manifest, nevertheless within the heart this light is revealed and shines well, and it has its effect in any case.

changes.before: At that time it is called in the Zohar “the moon in its deficiency”: the end of the month, when there is no completeness or light at all, only lack. Prayer was established for this condition. The twelve middle blessings include every kind of human need and lack, whose totality is twelve [corresponding to the twelve months of the lunar year]. These are the twelve tribes of God: each has a particular inborn lack [just as each also has a particular excellence], for which it must seek God’s salvation to complete it. Their totality is the congregation of Israel and the moon, as is known. [A thirteenth blessing was afterward instituted at Yavneh. Nevertheless it is still called the prayer of eighteen blessings, for the principal number is twelve, which sometimes becomes thirteen, as with the tribes and the months, when one becomes two. Likewise, among the thirteen measures of mercy surrounding her, one is doubled; see Tosafot, Rosh Hashanah 17b. This is not the place to elaborate.] Through prayer the person subjects all the powers of the soul to God: help comes only from Him, and from no other.

changes.before: For this [the sexual inclination] there is rescue through words of Torah, specifically when eating matzah on the night of Pesach has preceded it, to heal the prior appetite for food. The two are drawn from one another, as they said, “Filling the belly is among the evil forms [of conduct].” Eve’s eating from the Tree of Knowledge led to the serpent’s coming upon her afterward. This was the serpent’s instigation and counsel: through her failure in the appetite for food, he could prevail over her in this also. The reverse is likewise true: through matzah, which imparts holiness to eating, one also merits words of Torah in the holiness of restraint from sexual transgression. For the measure of good is greater; a mitzvah of eating all the more draws holiness in sexual matters, five hundredfold, according to the Sages’ statement in Makkot.

changes.before: This explains the Jerusalem Talmud’s statement: “Rabbi Matanya [the canonical Hebrew reads Rabbi Meir; the Jerusalem Talmud attributes this statement to Rabbi Matanya] said: I am grateful to my head, for when it reached Modim it bowed of itself.” How did the head sense that it should bow? If it was merely habit, why thank the head? The matter is that we say every blessing in the present tense: “Who grants knowledge,” “Who abundantly forgives,” “Who heals the sick.” When the person prays and God hears prayer, he is answered immediately, in the present. In Retzeh we bless “Who restores His presence to Zion,” in the present; through Moses’ holiness, to which this blessing corresponds, one merits this. Although the world is judged according to its majority and the community has not yet merited it, the individual soul praying has already been answered. This resembles “Anyone who has understanding is considered as though the Temple were built in his days.” When he senses that God is restoring His presence, fear immediately falls upon him, for “with great awe” means revelation of the Divine Presence. Wherever the Presence is revealed, fear and awe fall upon the person. The head senses this fear, like the master’s observation that the Talmud says “tefillin in the head,” rather than “upon the head,” meaning their illumination within the brain. Thus: “I am grateful to my head,” which senses the fear when it reaches Modim and bows of itself.

changes.before: This occurs through recognizing that the new teachings come from God. That is humility and acting for Heaven’s sake: the person recognizes that he has nothing of his own. He then succeeds and rises to the stature called “My mother.” For after the blessing and the recognition that everything comes from God, God says that everything belongs to him—even the awakening from above belongs to him. This is “Give strength [that is, words of Torah, as stated] to God”: it was through his awakening from below that this came into being.

changes.before: It would seem a defect to mix earthy matter into the supernal wisdom that rises to the place of seraphim and ofanim [angelic wheels] whose awe is a burning fire. What place does the slight awe of one born of woman, just as it is, have among them? Yet this is what God desires: He brought Torah down to those below and “cast truth to the earth.” The entire sustenance of the heavenly company comes from the Torah below. From the small awe produced by human effort, God builds a great storehouse with entrances as broad as the entrance of the Temple hall, as Shir HaShirim Rabbah says. All Torah and wisdom are afterward placed within the person’s heart. Chamṭin [earth used to preserve grain] becomes chiṭin [wheat]: the mem, alluding to kingship, is exchanged for a yod, alluding to wisdom; the small kav becomes a kor, and “Fear of the Lord is wisdom.”

changes.before: There is [a Holy Spirit] that comes through human preparation: a person prepares and sets boundaries for himself for the sake of God’s will, and through this attains the Holy Spirit. Thus the Midrash says, “Zeal brings to cleanliness ... piety brings to the Holy Spirit.” Through preparing himself with all the preparations the Midrash enumerates, he attains the Holy Spirit. This Holy Spirit is called prophecy needed for the generations, for since it came through human preparation, it remains established for the whole world.

changes.before: Within that order [as it stands from God’s side], a change of nature cannot be called a miracle or wonder. When that order shines, everyone sees explicitly that God gives life to creation at every moment. If the flow of life ceased for even a moment, the entire existence of creation would cease. How, then, can a particular change be called a wonder, when such a wonder is seen at every moment? It was like Adam immediately on the first day of his creation. Could he consider some newly seen thing a miracle, when everything was new to him and everything his eyes saw was a wonder? Seeing the sea moving and surging was itself a wonder to him. Only afterward, when he became accustomed to it and habit became nature, did it seem that nature required the sea always to move. If he then saw the sea stand still and become dry land, he would consider it a miracle because nature had changed. But when God opened Israel’s understanding to the true order as it is with Him, they recognized it in their own understanding just as Adam did immediately after creation: He who tells the sea to move can tell it not to move.

changes.before: Through humility one recognizes that God gives graciously, as in “I shall favor whom I favor”—even one who is not worthy. This may also be hinted at in “Esther found favor”: she recognized that everything comes from God through favor and kindness, and through this “Esther clothed herself in royalty,” which the Talmud and Zohar interpret as her clothing herself in the Holy Spirit, the aspect of Malchut. As explained, this is why she is the end of the miracles, corresponding to Malchut. The Midrash says that God created three gifts in the world: wisdom, strength, and wealth. We have explained that these correspond to life, children, and sustenance. Torah is the essence of life—“Wisdom gives life to its owner.” Strength corresponds to children, as in the mighty warriors who increased sons and grandsons; wealth corresponds to sustenance. The Midrash asks: when [are these good]? When they are gifts of Heaven. The essential thing is to recognize that they come from God as an unearned gift. Thus we say concerning wisdom, “You graciously grant ... graciously grant us from Yourself ... Who graciously grants knowledge.”

changes.before: This is a “wonder”—something wondrous and concealed. “Wonder” does not properly refer to the miracle itself: what wonder is it for God to perform a miracle? “He who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” Is the natural order not itself wondrous? God established it so, and when He wishes to change it, who can prevent Him? But “the Holy One does not perform a miracle for falsehood”: everything follows judgment. When it is not according to [the apparent] judgment, that is called a wonder—performing a miracle for someone not worthy of it. This occurs only through the revelation of the supreme wonder, the wondrous place to which Israel is bound, having arisen first in thought: the depth of the beginning of thought, the nothingness preceding the being within thought. They are the seed of truth, and “truth is Torah”; whoever is bound to Torah is bound to everything, to the head of all degrees.

changes.before: [Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair] said to the River Ginnai: it is true that a person possesses choice and is therefore called only “one who may accomplish.” Yet within that uncertainty of choice, I carry out His will more than you do in certainty. We possess choice; moreover, when the evil inclination is present, no one recalls the good inclination. A person could even remain without choice and say, like the creatures without choice, “The Lord is mighty on high.” Yet I do not wish to rely on the assurance that God directs me without my choice, beyond my understanding, merely saying “The Lord is mighty on high.” I continually work to fulfill His will within my own understanding and bring the Divine Presence down into my actions, so as to perform His will through my good choice. Justice therefore also requires that my uncertain act displace your certain one. In the place of my choice you have no dealings with God, whereas I continually deal with Him, illuminating through my service even a place without choice and restraining myself there too through my good choice. Joseph’s coffin alludes to this restraint. Therefore the Sages say, “The sea saw and fled”—it saw Joseph’s coffin and fled.
